::: {#exm-simulate-variance-bias}
#### Simulating the bias of the divide-by-$n$ variance estimator

For the [data-generating process](#exm-data-generating-process) with $\mean = 0$, $\varpar = 4$ and $n = 10$,
we simulate the [bias](estimation.qmd#def-bias) of the divide-by-$n$ [estimator](estimation.qmd#def-estimator) $\hvarpar$ of $\varpar$
from [the example of a biased variance estimator](estimation.qmd#exm-biased-variance-mle).
That example shows that the bias is exactly $-\varpar / n = -0.4$,
so the simulation can be checked against the known answer.

Each [replication](#def-replication) draws $n = 10$ values and computes one [estimate](estimation.qmd#def-estimate) of $\varpar$.
We run $M = 10000$ [replications](#def-replication),
set the [seed](#def-seed) once at the start,
and report the [simulation estimate](#def-simulation-estimate) of the bias with its [Monte Carlo standard error](#def-monte-carlo-standard-error).
The choice $M = 10000$ gives a Monte Carlo standard error of about $0.02$,
small next to the bias.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

##### R

```{r}
#| label: simulate-variance-bias-r
#| code-fold: false
n <- 10
sigma_sq <- 4
n_reps <- 10000
n_draws <- n_reps * n

set.seed(571)
draws <- rnorm(n_draws, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(sigma_sq))
# Each row is one replication's data set.
x <- matrix(draws, nrow = n_reps)

x_bar <- rowMeans(x)
deviations <- x - x_bar
squared_deviations <- deviations^2
var_hat <- rowMeans(squared_deviations)

bias_hat <- mean(var_hat) - sigma_sq
mc_se <- sd(var_hat) / sqrt(n_reps)

c(
  simulation_estimate = bias_hat,
  mc_standard_error = mc_se,
  known_bias = -sigma_sq / n
)
```

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: simulate-variance-bias-py
#| code-fold: false
import numpy as np

n = 10
sigma_sq = 4
n_reps = 10000

rng = np.random.default_rng(571)
# Each row is one replication's data set.
x = rng.normal(loc=0, scale=np.sqrt(sigma_sq), size=(n_reps, n))

x_bar = x.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
var_hat = ((x - x_bar) ** 2).mean(axis=1)

bias_hat = var_hat.mean() - sigma_sq
mc_se = var_hat.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_reps)

print(f"simulation estimate: {bias_hat:.3f}")
print(f"mc standard error:   {mc_se:.3f}")
print(f"known bias:          {-sigma_sq / n:.3f}")
```

:::

The R [simulation estimate](#def-simulation-estimate) of the [bias](estimation.qmd#def-bias) is `r round(bias_hat, 3)`,
with a [Monte Carlo standard error](#def-monte-carlo-standard-error) of `r round(mc_se, 3)`.
It is within `r round(abs(bias_hat - (-sigma_sq / n)) / mc_se, 1)` [Monte Carlo standard errors](#def-monte-carlo-standard-error) of the known bias $-0.4$.
The Python run uses a different random number generator,
so its [estimate](estimation.qmd#def-estimate) differs slightly,
but it too agrees with $-0.4$ up to its Monte Carlo standard error.

@fig-simulate-variance-bias shows the [sampling distribution](estimation.qmd#def-sampling-distribution) of $\hvarpar$ that the [replications](#def-replication) trace out.
Its [histogram](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-histogram) uses 40 equal-width [bins](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-bin),
which put about 250 of the 10000 [estimates](estimation.qmd#def-estimate) in the average [bin](exploratory-descriptive.qmd#def-bin).
Fewer bins, such as 10, would hide the right skew of the distribution in a few wide bars.
More bins, such as 200, would leave about 50 estimates per bin on average,
and random bar-to-bar variation would hide the shape.
The bin count changes only the picture, not any number reported above.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simulate-variance-bias
#| fig-cap: "Estimates of the variance from 10,000 replications. The vertical lines mark the true variance 4 and the average estimate, which falls below it by the bias."
#| fig-alt: "A histogram of 10,000 divide-by-n variance estimates, right-skewed, with one vertical line at the true variance 4 and a second, slightly to its left, at the average estimate."
#| code-fold: true
estimates <- data.frame(var_hat = var_hat)
means <- data.frame(
  value = c(sigma_sq, mean(var_hat)),
  line = c("True variance", "Average estimate")
)

ggplot(estimates) +
  aes(x = var_hat) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey80", color = "grey40") + # check-unexplained-choices: allow
  geom_vline(
    data = means,
    mapping = aes(xintercept = value, linetype = line)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Estimate of the variance", y = "Replications", linetype = NULL)
```

The distribution is right-skewed,
and its average sits below the true [variance](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#def-variance),
which is the bias.
:::
